t: "We are writing" or "we write to you"?
p: The Byzantine text and the KJV read "these things write we unto you".

readings.w: Sinaiticus (01, 300s), Alexandrinus as first written (02, 400s), Vaticanus (03, 300s), P, Ψ, 33, part of the Sahidic Coptic; SBLGNT, NA28 (ECM), Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort

Alexandrinus as corrected, Ephraemi (C, 04, 400s), K, L, 81, 1739, the Byzantine majority, the Old Latin and Vulgate, the Syriac Peshitta and Harklean, the Bohairic Coptic, Augustine; Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.en: and these things we write to you
readings.plain: We are writing these things to you

why: The oldest manuscripts have the emphatic "we". "To you" is the expected phrase in a letter (2:1, 7, 12-14), so copyists were likely to add it, and less likely to replace it with an unusual "we".

p: The KJV has "that your joy may be full". The evidence is close; NA28 marks both readings as possible.

readings.w: Sinaiticus (01), Vaticanus (03), L, Ψ, 049, many Byzantine manuscripts, the Sahidic Coptic, the Vulgate in its critical editions, Stephanus' Greek text of 1550; SBLGNT, NA28 (text), Westcott-Hort

Alexandrinus (02), Ephraemi (04), K, P, 33, 81, 1739, many Byzantine manuscripts, the Clementine Vulgate, the Harklean Syriac, the Bohairic Coptic, Augustine; Scrivener's Textus Receptus (KJV); NA28 and the ECM give it equal weight (a split line)

why: "Our" has slightly older support and is the less expected reading. "Your joy" may have come in from Jesus' words in John 16:24 ("so that your joy will be filled up"), which copyists knew well. The NET Bible prefers "our" but notes that NA28 and UBS5 now treat "your" as equally possible.
b: The two words differ by one letter in Greek (hēmōn, hymōn), and the Byzantine manuscripts themselves are split between them.

p: The Byzantine text and the KJV read "the blood of Jesus Christ his Son".

Alexandrinus (02), 33, the Byzantine majority, the Clementine Vulgate, the Harklean Syriac, the Bohairic Coptic; Textus Receptus (KJV)

why: The fuller name is the kind of addition copyists made to honor Jesus, and the shorter text has the older and wider support.
b: There is a second, smaller difference here. NA28 leaves out the opening "But" (de), while NA27, SBLGNT, the Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles, the Textus Receptus and the Byzantine text have it (the editions marked in this site's word list). The Plain English Translation keeps "But" with SBLGNT; the contrast with 1:6 is clear either way.

a: Children, I have written to you
p: In the Byzantine text and the KJV the third line of 2:13 reads "I write unto you, little children".

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles (the editions marked in this site's word list)

readings.plain: Children, I have written to you

readings.w: The Byzantine text (Robinson-Pierpont); Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.en: I am writing to you, children
readings.plain: Children, I am writing to you

why: The editions based on the oldest manuscripts begin the second set of three lines here, with "I have written". The Byzantine text makes the third line match the two before it ("I am writing"), which gives four "I am writing" lines (2:12 and three in 2:13) and two "I have written" lines (2:14). The critical text's pattern, three "I am writing" and three "I have written", is the harder and likelier one.

t: "You all know" or "you know all things"?
p: The KJV has "ye know all things". The oldest manuscripts say "you all know".

readings.w: Sinaiticus (01), Vaticanus (03), P, Ψ, 1852, the Sahidic Coptic, Jerome; SBLGNT, NA28, Westcott-Hort
Alexandrinus (02), Ephraemi (04), K, L, 33, 81, 1739, the Byzantine majority, the Old Latin and Vulgate, the Bohairic Coptic; Textus Receptus (KJV)

why: The writer's point is that all the readers, not only an inner circle, have knowledge, against teachers who claimed a higher knowledge for a few. Raymond Brown, quoted in the NET Bible note, puts it this way: "the fact of their knowledge (pantes), not the extent of its object (panta), seems best to fit the reassurance". "All things" may have come from 2:27, "about all things".
b: The NET Bible judges the evidence "solidly, though not overwhelmingly, behind the nominative reading". Compare Jeremiah 31:34, where the Greek (38:34 in the Septuagint) promises that all "will know" the Lord.

a: Anyone who confesses the Son has the Father too.
t: Why the KJV printed this sentence in italics
p: The Byzantine text skips this sentence. The KJV of 1611 printed it in small type as words not in its Greek.

readings.en: the one who confesses the Son has the Father also
readings.plain: Anyone who confesses the Son has the Father too.

readings.w: K, L, the Byzantine majority, Stephanus' Greek text of 1550

why: The two halves of the verse both end with the words "has the Father" (ton patera echei), so a copyist's eye could easily jump from the first ending to the second and drop the sentence between them (haplography). The oldest manuscripts all have it.
b: The 1611 KJV printed the whole phrase "but he that acknowledgeth the Sonne, hath the Father also" in small type, which it used for words not in the original; later printings use italics for the same purpose (P. J. Williams).

p: The KJV reads "He that loveth not his brother abideth in death".

p: Ancient Latin copies and some fathers read "every spirit that separates (or dissolves) Jesus".

readings.w: Alexandrinus (02), Vaticanus (03), 1739 (text) and other Greek manuscripts; SBLGNT, NA28, Westcott-Hort. Sinaiticus (01) has "Jesus as Lord come in the flesh"
K, L, 049, the Byzantine manuscripts; Textus Receptus (KJV, "confesseth not that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh")
readings.orig: μὴ ὁμολογεῖ [τὸν] Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν ἐν σαρκὶ ἐληλυθότα
readings.en: does not confess Jesus Christ having come in the flesh
readings.plain: does not confess Jesus Christ as having come in the flesh

readings.w: No Greek manuscript in its text. A note in the margin of 1739 (which credits Irenaeus, Clement and Origen); the Old Latin and the Vulgate (qui solvit Iesum, Clementine edition); Irenaeus in Latin; Tertullian; Origen in Latin; Lucifer; Priscillian; and "the ancient copies" known to Socrates the historian

why: "Does not confess" is in every Greek manuscript's text and matches the positive "confesses" of 4:2. The longer Byzantine wording copies 4:2. "Separates Jesus" is old, but it survives almost only in Latin and in the fathers, and it reads like a sharpening of the verse against teachers who split Jesus from the Christ.
b: Irenaeus (about 180) quotes it: "every spirit which separates Jesus Christ is not of God, but is of antichrist" (Against Heresies 3.16.8). Socrates (400s) says that "in the ancient copies" it read "Every spirit that separates Jesus, is not of God", and blames the change on those "who desired to separate the Divine nature from the human economy" (Church History 7.32). The Catholic Church's Nova Vulgata now reads qui non confitetur Iesum, "who does not confess Jesus". The longer wording is close to Polycarp's letter to the Philippians (about 110-135): "For whosoever does not confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh, is antichrist" (Philippians 7), which shows the phrase in use early, though Polycarp is quoting freely, not copying a manuscript.

t: "We love", "we love him" or "we love God"?
p: The KJV reads "We love him, because he first loved us".

a: For those who testify are three:
t: The Johannine Comma: "in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost"
p: The KJV's "three that bear record in heaven" is not in any Greek manuscript before the 1300s. It goes with 5:8.

readings.w: Sinaiticus (01, 300s), Alexandrinus (02, 400s), Vaticanus (03, 300s), every other Greek manuscript before the 1300s, the Byzantine majority; the oldest Vulgate manuscripts (Fuldensis, AD 546, and Amiatinus); the Syriac, Coptic, Ethiopic, Georgian and Arabic versions; Greek and Latin writers including Irenaeus, Tertullian, Athanasius, Basil, Gregory of Nazianzus, Hilary, Jerome and Augustine; SBLGNT, NA28, the Nova Vulgata
readings.en: For there are three who testify
readings.plain: For those who testify are three:

readings.w: Greek, in the text: minuscules 629 (1300s-1400s, Greek and Latin side by side), 918 (1500s), 61 (Codex Montfortianus, about 1520), 2473 (1600s), 2318 (1700s); added in the margin of 221, 177, 88, 429 and 636, mostly by much later hands; first in Greek in the Greek translation of the Acts of the Lateran Council of 1215. Latin: Priscillian's Liber Apologeticus (about 380), Old Latin copies from Spain (the León palimpsest, 600s; the Freising fragments), later Vulgate manuscripts, the Sixtine (1590) and Clementine (1592) Vulgate. In print: the Complutensian Polyglot (Greek and Latin; its New Testament was printed in 1514, but the work was not published until 1520-1521), Erasmus' third edition (1522) and the Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.orig: ὅτι τρεῖς εἰσιν οἱ μαρτυροῦντες ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ, ὁ πατήρ, ὁ λόγος, καὶ τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμα, καὶ οὗτοι οἱ τρεῖς ἕν εἰσιν
readings.en: For there are three that testify in heaven: the Father, the Word and the Holy Spirit, and these three are one
readings.plain: For those who testify in heaven are three: the Father, the Word and the Holy Spirit; and these three are one.

why: The added words are missing from every Greek manuscript for over a thousand years, from the oldest Vulgate copies, and from every ancient version except the Latin. Greek fathers of the 300s who wrote at length on the Trinity, such as Athanasius, Basil and Gregory of Nazianzus, never quote the added words: they are listed for the shorter text because of that silence, which would be strange if the words had been in their Bibles. The words first appear in Latin; in the NET Bible's judgment they "seem to have arisen in a fourth century Latin homily in which the text was allegorized to refer to members of the Trinity", and moved from there into Vulgate copies. Translations based on the critical text have left them out of the main text since the English Revised Version of 1881, and the Catholic Church's Nova Vulgata leaves them out too.
b: The Greek manuscripts that have the words in the text were written after 1300, and Codex 61's wording was translated from the Latin. The NET Bible notes that the marginal note in 177 "must be dated after 1551". See the deep dive on the chapter page for the history: Priscillian, Erasmus, the KJV, Newton, and the Catholic rulings of 1897 and 1927.

why: The shorter text has the older witnesses. The awkward words at the end ("to you who believe") were moved forward to smooth the sentence, and the last clause was added from John 20:31 ("so that you may believe").

p: The Greek has "himself" or "him". With "him", the one born from God may be Christ, keeping the believer.

readings.w: Sinaiticus (01), Alexandrinus as corrected, K, L, P, Ψ, 33, 81, 1739, the Byzantine majority, the Syriac Peshitta, Origen; NA28 and the ECM, Tyndale House GNT, Textus Receptus (KJV "keepeth himself")
Alexandrinus as first written (02), Vaticanus (03), 614, 1505, the Old Latin and Vulgate, the Harklean Syriac, the Bohairic Coptic, Jerome; SBLGNT, Westcott-Hort, NA27

why: The Plain English Translation follows NA28, whose text in the Catholic Letters is taken from the Editio Critica Maior; "himself" has the wider support. But the question is close: Peter Head writes that "both readings are well attested", and the NET Bible prefers "him" as the harder reading, which a copyist might change to "himself" to smooth the grammar.
b: The Latin versions, among them the Vulgate (generatio Dei conservat eum, Clementine edition), three Greek minuscules (1505, 1852, 2138) and the Bohairic Coptic read "the birth from God keeps him"; the NET Bible calls this evidence "extremely slight". The reading avoids the question of who "the one born" is. On the meaning, see the note on "the one born from God".
